items.scenario: You ask Claude to 'write a SubscriptionService' for a Spring Boot codebase. The result uses field injection and RuntimeException, while your codebase uses constructor injection and a typed Result pattern. Review stalls on style.
items.question: What change to the prompt would most reliably fix this next time?
options: Add 'follow Spring Boot best practices and clean-code principles' to the prompt
Supply the conventions, lint rules and sibling OrderService.java as a sample
Switch to a higher effort level so it reasons more carefully about house style
Ask for the code in smaller pieces, one method per prompt, reviewing each
items.explanation: Generated code fits the codebase only when the codebase is in the context. A sibling file plus written conventions and lint rules transfers the house style; Claude otherwise defaults to the average of public code.
distractors: 'Best practices' are the generic public defaults — exactly what produced field injection.
Effort doesn't supply information Claude doesn't have; your conventions are context, not reasoning.
Smaller pieces still have no sample to imitate, so each piece is generic.

items.scenario: A teammate needs a new reporting module touching six files. They plan to ask Claude for the full implementation in one prompt and review the 600-line diff afterwards.
items.question: What is the better approach?
options: Ask for the full implementation but at maximum effort so the diff is right first time
Ask for the implementation file by file, reviewing each before the next
Ask first for the file list, signatures and error handling, review that, then implement
Ask for the implementation and then ask Claude to review its own diff
items.explanation: Plan-before-code catches architecture mistakes (wrong layer, a missed existing utility) when they're a ten-line correction, not a 600-line rework.
distractors: Higher effort doesn't let you review the approach before it's built; a wrong architecture at max effort is still wrong.
File by file without an agreed plan risks each file assuming a different design.
Self-review is a filter, not a guarantee, and it still happens after the expensive work is done.

items.scenario: Claude explains a password-validation regex in your auth service and says it requires 'at least 12 characters, one digit and one capital letter'. You're about to quote this in a security review.
items.question: What should you do before quoting it?
options: Ask Claude to re-read the regex carefully and confirm its explanation
Ask for strings that should match and fail, then run them against the regex
Ask a second model to explain the same regex and compare the two explanations
Quote it in the doc with a clear note that the explanation was AI-generated
items.explanation: An explanation of a regex is a claim; the regex engine is the oracle. Running should-match and should-fail cases tests the explanation directly.
distractors: Asking the same model to confirm itself mostly gets agreement, not evidence.
Two explanations agreeing is still two claims; neither is a test.
Disclosure doesn't make an unverified claim correct in a security review.

items.scenario: On a client's undocumented monolith, Claude reads a pricing module and writes: 'This function applies a legacy loyalty discount for pre-2019 accounts.' You're writing the handover documentation.
items.question: How should this statement go into the documentation?
options: Verbatim, since the function name and comments clearly support it
Removed, because inferred intent shouldn't be documented
Rewritten in your own words so it doesn't read as AI-generated output
As a labelled inference until confirmed by callers, tests or history
items.explanation: Inferred intent is a hypothesis. Separate what the code does from what it is probably for, and confirm the latter before publishing — otherwise someone later 'fixes' deliberate behaviour or trusts a wrong one.
distractors: Plausible names and comments are exactly what make a wrong inference convincing.
Inferences are valuable for a handover; they just need labelling and confirming.
Rewording doesn't change whether the claim is verified.

items.scenario: Converting a Java service to Kotlin, Claude produces code full of getX() calls and !! operators. It compiles and the tests pass.
items.question: What is the main problem and the right follow-up?
options: It's transliterated; ask for idiomatic Kotlin plus a list of what didn't map one-to-one
Nothing, since the tests pass and the conversion is therefore complete
The !! operators are fine, but the getters must be renamed to match Kotlin style
The conversion should be redone in Java-compatible Kotlin for interop safety with callers
items.explanation: Transliteration keeps Java idioms in Kotlin syntax; !! hides nulls the type system could catch. Idiomatic translation plus an explicit 'could not convert' list is the standard.
distractors: Passing tests don't make !! safe; each one is a possible NPE the tests didn't exercise, and the code is unmaintainable Kotlin.
!! is the more serious issue — it disables null safety at runtime.
'Java-compatible Kotlin' is the transliteration problem, not a fix.

items.scenario: A Python 2 → 3 conversion of a file-ingestion module 'works' on the sample files, but production files from one client contain non-ASCII names.
items.question: Which area of the conversion most needs a human decision and a test here?
options: Replacing print statements with print() function calls
Rewriting each except X, e clause as except X as e
The str/bytes boundary where files are read and decoded
Replacing dict.iteritems() with dict.items() in loops
items.explanation: str/bytes handling is the Python 2→3 change that can't be converted mechanically: encodings must be decided where bytes enter the system, and only data like the client's will expose it.
distractors: print conversion is purely mechanical and doesn't affect encoding.
Exception syntax is mechanical and behaviour-neutral.
iteritems → items is mechanical; it doesn't touch text decoding.

items.scenario: Claude generates a DTO-to-entity mapper for a 40-field customer record. It compiles, and a quick read looks right.
items.question: What is the most effective check before merging?
options: Ask Claude to list every field it mapped and confirm none were skipped
Add a round-trip test that maps a fully populated object and compares every field
Run the linter with its strictest rules on the generated mapper file and fix the warnings
Compare the field count of the DTO and the entity to confirm they match
items.explanation: Mappers fail silently — swapped or dropped fields compile and look plausible. A round-trip test on a fully populated object catches both.
distractors: Claude's list is another claim; it would describe the swap as correct.
Linters don't know that firstName shouldn't map to lastName.
Equal field counts don't detect a swapped mapping.

items.scenario: A Node.js job Claude wrote logs 'done' and exits, but only some welcome emails are sent. The code is: users.forEach(async u => { await sendEmail(u) }); console.log('done').
items.question: What is the defect?
options: sendEmail must be wrapped in a try/catch so failures are logged instead of swallowed
console.log runs before the logger flushes and should be a structured logger
The enclosing function must be declared async so the inner awaits can run
forEach doesn't await async callbacks, so the job ends before the sends complete
items.explanation: Array.forEach ignores returned promises. Use for…of with await, or Promise.all with a concurrency limit, so the job waits.
distractors: Error handling matters but doesn't explain why sends are cut off.
Swapping the logger doesn't change whether the email promises are awaited.
Making the outer function async doesn't make forEach await its callbacks; forEach still discards the promises.

items.scenario: Migrating a reporting database from SQL Server to PostgreSQL, Claude converts TOP to LIMIT, ISNULL to COALESCE and GETDATE() to now(). All queries run. Finance later finds a customer search that used to match 'ACME' and 'acme' now misses one.
items.question: What should the conversion checklist have flagged?
options: Collation and case-sensitivity differences between the two databases
COALESCE evaluating its arguments differently from ISNULL
LIMIT needing an ORDER BY to return the same rows each time
now() returning a timezone-aware value where GETDATE() did not
items.explanation: Default SQL Server collations are typically case-insensitive while PostgreSQL comparisons are case-sensitive by default — a semantic difference no syntax rewrite catches. It belongs on the 'cannot convert mechanically' list.
distractors: ISNULL/COALESCE differences exist (typing) but don't explain case-sensitive matching.
ORDER BY with LIMIT matters for determinism, not for case matching.
The timestamp type does differ, but it doesn't affect matching 'ACME' against 'acme'.

items.scenario: A pre-sales team used Claude to build a Next.js demo for a client in two days. After the demo, a product manager proposes merging it into the product 'since it already works'.
items.question: What is the right response?
options: Merge it, but run Claude over it once more to tidy the code and fix the conventions
Merge it behind a feature flag so it can be switched off if problems appear
Treat it as a prototype: rebuild it or bring it in through normal review and tests
Merge only the UI components, since they are lower risk than the backend code
items.explanation: Demo code was generated without the codebase's conventions, tests or review. It enters the product only through the same process as any other code.
distractors: Another generation pass isn't review; ownership of correctness stays with a human.
A flag limits exposure but still ships unreviewed, untested code into the product.
UI components carry their own risks (accessibility, state bugs) and still skipped review.
